model.name: Legal Entity Registration
model.purpose: Represent the legal identity, formation jurisdiction, authoritative registers, identifiers and lifecycle of a registered legal person so an agent can create, inspect and operate registration records independently of storage format.
model.scope_statement: This model covers a legally distinct person that is constituted under a jurisdiction's law, bound to one or more authoritative registers, identified by register-assigned and optional global identifiers, classified by a jurisdiction-specific legal form, and subject to status, events, disclosure, validation and retention rules from formation through dissolution or nullity. It is an alignment to ISO 17442, ISO 20275, EU company-law registers, FATF Recommendation 24 and UNCITRAL limited-liability formation rules, not a claim of a single worldwide company code.
in_scope: Legal personality, capacity to contract and asset partitioning of a registered legal person, including companies, partnerships constituted as legal persons, funds, governmental and supranational bodies, international branches eligible under ISO 17442, and individuals acting in a business capacity where a jurisdiction treats them as registerable legal entities.

Authoritative business, commercial, companies and comparable registration authorities; the register file; national and European unique identifiers; the Legal Entity Identifier and its Level 1 reference data.
Jurisdiction of legal formation, ISO 20275 entity legal form, registered office or legal address of formation, headquarters address, and registered branches or establishments.

Constituting instruments, disclosed particulars, persons authorised to bind the entity, legal-owner or member registers required as basic company information, and legal-entity events that change identity, form, status or succession.

Entity status versus identifier-registration status, formation and expiration dates, dissolution, winding-up, liquidation, insolvency effects on the register, merger, conversion, nullity and successor entities.

Corroboration against the local authoritative source, public and competent-authority access to basic information, the obligation to hold adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial-ownership information, and retention after the entity ceases to exist.
out_of_scope: The social or operational organisation as a going concern (parent WM-ORG-001), including informal groups that lack legal personality.
Natural persons in a private capacity; FATF legal arrangements such as express trusts (Recommendation 25) except where a trust is itself registered as a legal person.

The beneficial-ownership graph, control percentages, nominee-arrangement mechanics and politically exposed-person screening beyond the existence, location, quality and access rules of the legal-person transparency obligation.
Insolvency case administration, creditor ranking, going-concern sale and discharge, except as register-visible events and status transitions.
Tax assessment, accounting standards, securities issuance, employment, licences to operate, sanctions screening and contractual performance.
Full officer, shareholder or member master data as person records; this model stores only register particulars and links.

boundary_notes.distinction: The parent organisation model describes an organisation as a social and operational actor. This model is the legal-person registration facet: personality conferred by law, the register that proves it, and the lifecycle of that proof. An organisation may exist without this facet; a registered legal person must have it.

FATF Recommendation 24 and its Interpretive Note require basic company information in the company registry and a multi-pronged beneficial-ownership mechanism. This model records the obligation, the company-registry basic set, the holding body, access and retention. The ownership/control graph itself is a sibling, not duplicated here.

Recommendation 25 addresses legal arrangements, not legal persons. Trusts and similar arrangements are out of scope unless a jurisdiction registers them as legal persons with a legal form and register identifier.

UNCITRAL insolvency guidance treats liquidation as typically ending in dissolution of a legal person. This model records insolvency, liquidation and dissolution as register events and status; it does not model the proceeding, estate or creditor process.

boundary_notes.neighbor: Natural person and official organisational role
boundary_notes.distinction: Directors, legal representatives and applicants appear here only as disclosed register particulars. Person identity, ISO 5009 roles and authority to act as a human agent belong in person/role models.
FATF lists a unique identifier such as a tax identification number as company-registry basic information. The identifier as a register key is in scope; tax residence, assessment and filing are not.

Registered office, legal address of formation and headquarters are legal-seat attributes of the registration record. Geocoding, premises and operational sites beyond those legal addresses are a location sibling.

sources.title: ISO 17442-1:2020 Financial services — Legal entity identifier (LEI) — Part 1: Assignment
sources.relevance: Defines the eligible legal-entity population, the 20-character LEI, and the minimum identification scheme for parties that can enter contracts or bear financial responsibility, including governmental bodies, supranationals, international branches and individuals acting in a business capacity, excluding natural persons in a private capacity.

sources.title: LEI-CDF Version 3.1 documentation and Level 1 Data: LEI-CDF Format 3.1
sources.version_or_date: LEI-CDF 3.1 (May 2021); documentation last updated 2021-03-04; business rules referenced 2025-07-03 v2.8.5
sources.relevance: Operationalises ISO 17442 attributes as Level 1 reference data: legal name, registration authority and entity ID, legal form, legal jurisdiction, legal and headquarters addresses, entity status, creation and expiration, legal-entity event effective dates, and LEI registration status, validation and update metadata.

sources.title: Directive (EU) 2017/1132 relating to certain aspects of company law (codified, consolidated)
sources.organization: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
sources.relevance: Normative EU rules on incorporation disclosure, the companies register file, European unique identifier (EUID), registered office, constituting instruments, persons authorised to bind, winding-up, nullity, liquidators, branches, online procedures and the Business Registers Interconnection System (BRIS).

sources.title: The FATF Recommendations — Recommendation 24 and Interpretive Note (Transparency and beneficial ownership of legal persons)
sources.relevance: Requires company registration, a published basic-information set, a multi-pronged beneficial-ownership mechanism, controls on bearer shares and nominees, competent-authority access, and at least five-year retention after dissolution.

sources.title: UNCITRAL Legislative Guide on Limited Liability Enterprises
sources.organization: United Nations Commission on International Trade Law
sources.version_or_date: Adopted 2021; United Nations publication 2022, Sales No. E.22.V.21
sources.relevance: Recommends distinct legal personality, limited liability, constitutive registration (the LLE is formed once registered), minimum formation particulars, identity and visibility through a business registry, conversion/restructuring and dissolution, and points to the 2018 UNCITRAL Guide on Key Principles of a Business Registry.

sources.title: ISO 20275 Entity Legal Forms (ELF) Code List
sources.organization: Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation as maintenance publication of ISO 20275
sources.version_or_date: ISO 20275:2017; ELF Code List Version 1.6, February 2026
sources.relevance: Jurisdiction-specific four-character legal-form codes; more than 3,600 forms across more than 200 jurisdictions; codes carry no embedded intelligence and are not equivalent across countries.

sources.title: GLEIF Registration Authorities List
sources.relevance: Codes more than 1,050 business registers and validation authorities in 232 jurisdictions, including reserved codes RA777777 (PUBLIC LEGAL DOCUMENT for general government entities), RA888888 and RA999999.

sources.title: Global LEI System
sources.organization: Legal Entity Identifier Regulatory Oversight Committee
sources.version_or_date: Page describing GLEIS governance; ISO 17442 originally 30 May 2012; accessed 2026-08-24
sources.relevance: Defines GLEIS governance (ROC, GLEIF, Local Operating Units), the 20-character LEI structure, uniqueness, and the right to port an LEI between operators without changing the code.

sources.title: UNCITRAL Legislative Guide on Insolvency Law
sources.organization: United Nations Commission on International Trade Law
sources.version_or_date: Parts one and two 25 June 2004; subsequent parts 2010–2021
sources.relevance: States that a corporation obtains legal personality by a legal process, enjoys perpetuity independent of members, and that liquidation of a commercial legal entity usually results in its dissolution.

sources.title: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/2244 laying down technical specifications and procedures for the system of interconnection of registers
sources.relevance: Specifies BRIS message exchange, EUID as the unique identifier of the company, and Alternate ID including Legal Entity Identifier for cross-register notifications such as branch disclosure.

sources.title: Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons (Recommendation 24)
sources.relevance: Explains the multi-pronged approach, holding of beneficial-ownership information by a public authority or an alternative mechanism, verification, and treatment of foreign-created legal persons with sufficient links.

sources.title: GLEIF Base Ontology
sources.relevance: Formalises EntityStatus, EntityExpirationReason (corporate action, dissolved, other) and RegistrationAuthority as first-party semantics for legal-entity registration records.

bundles.name: Legal identity and personality
bundles.description: Who the registered legal person is: the fact of legal personality, the eligible party types, the official name, and the identifiers that uniquely denote the entity in the formation register and optionally in the Global LEI System.
bundles.rationale: ISO 17442, GLEIF Level 1 data, EU company-law disclosure and UNCITRAL LLE recommendations all start from a legally distinct person with an official name and at least one authoritative identifier. Without this bundle an agent cannot tell a registered legal person from an informal organisation or a natural person.

layers.name: Legal personality and eligible types
layers.description: The legal fact of personality, asset partitioning and the population that may be registered or assigned an LEI.

findings.name: Legal personality and capacity
findings.description: A registered legal person is a juristic person distinct from its members, able to acquire rights and assume obligations in its own name. UNCITRAL treats this as affirmative asset partitioning and recommends that members are not personally liable solely by reason of membership. UNCITRAL insolvency guidance adds that a corporation obtains personality by a legal process and enjoys perpetuity independent of changing members. ISO 17442 requires the party to have the legal right in its jurisdiction to enter independently into legal contracts.

questions.text: Does this subject have legal personality distinct from its members or controllers under the law of the formation jurisdiction?
Which capacities does the law confer on this legal person, and are any of them restricted by statute, objects or duration?
Are members or shareholders shielded from the entity's debts solely by reason of membership, and under which legal form rule?
At what event time did legal personality attach, and is registration constitutive or merely declaratory in this jurisdiction?

data_elements.name: Has legal personality
data_elements.description: Whether the subject is a juristic person distinct from natural-person members.

data_elements.name: Personality effective at
data_elements.description: Event time at which legal personality attached under the formation law, recorded separately from observation or ingestion time.

data_elements.name: Formation theory
data_elements.description: Whether registration creates the person (UNCITRAL LLE Recommendation 8: formed once registered) or records a person already constituted.

data_elements.name: Member liability regime
data_elements.description: Limited, unlimited or mixed liability of members solely by reason of membership.

artifacts.name: Proof of incorporation or constitution
artifacts.description: Certificate, extract or statutory instrument that proves the entity exists as a legal person. FATF INR 24 lists proof of incorporation in the company-registry basic set.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Authoritative register document number in the formation jurisdiction; Dimension UUID only if the register issues no document identifier.

findings.name: Eligible party types
findings.description: ISO 17442 applies to unique parties legally or financially responsible for financial transactions or able to contract independently, including governmental organisations, supranationals, international branches and individuals acting in a business capacity, and excludes natural persons in a private capacity. GLEIF EntityCategory distinguishes general entities, funds, sole proprietors, branches and international organisations. FATF Recommendation 24 applies to all forms of legal persons, with company rules applied mutatis mutandis. Partnerships or MSMEs without personality are a different legal object.

questions.text: Which ISO 17442 / GLEIF entity category and, if any, subcategory describe this registered party?
Is the subject a natural person in a private capacity and therefore outside this model, or a sole trader or similar business-capacity registration?
If the subject is a partnership, association, fund or government body, does the formation law confer legal personality or only a register entry without personality?

data_elements.name: Entity category
data_elements.description: GLEIF/ISO 17442 category of the legal entity (for example GENERAL, FUND, SOLE_PROPRIETOR, BRANCH, INTERNATIONAL_ORGANIZATION).

data_elements.name: Entity subcategory
data_elements.description: Optional finer GLEIF subcategory where the CDF provides one.

data_elements.name: Is international branch
data_elements.description: Whether the record is an international branch eligible for an LEI under ISO 17442-1:2020 clause 3.5 rather than a separately incorporated legal person.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Category and eligibility are coded reference data on the registration record; they are not independent documents. Supporting evidence lives on the proof-of-incorporation and register-file artefacts of sibling findings.

layers.name: Official name and identifiers
layers.description: The name as recorded in the official register or constituting documents, and the master and global identifiers.

findings.name: Official legal name
findings.description: ISO 17442 and GLEIF Level 1 require the name of the legal entity as recorded in an official register, or otherwise in constituting documents. EU disclosure requires the name or names and legal form. Names may have language tags, transliterations, previous legal names and trading names. Name changes are legal-entity events with an effective date in the formation jurisdiction.

questions.text: What is the official legal name as recorded in the authoritative register or constituting instrument, in which language?
Which transliterated, previous, trading or additional registered names apply, and over which validity interval?
answer_data: collection other_names {text, code name_type, code language, timestamp valid_from, timestamp valid_to}

questions.text: Does the name satisfy jurisdiction rules against misleading form, public-policy conflict and collision with existing registered names?

data_elements.name: Legal name
data_elements.description: Official name as recorded in the register or constituting documents.

data_elements.name: Legal name language
data_elements.description: Language of the official name, typically as xml:lang on the LEI-CDF LegalName.

data_elements.name: Other entity names
data_elements.description: Transliterated legal names, previous legal names and trading or operating names.

artifacts.name: Name registration entry
artifacts.description: Register entry or naming decision that records the official name and any refused or previous names.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register entry identifier plus effective date of the name; not the date alone.

findings.name: Authoritative and global identifiers
findings.description: Identity priority is the identifier assigned by the incorporating or other authoritative register, then a governed global identifier (LEI or EUID), then a Dimension-assigned UUID/ULID. ISO 17442 specifies a 20-character alphanumeric LEI with LOU prefix, reserved characters, entity section and check digits. LEI ROC requires uniqueness (one LEI per entity) and allows porting between LOUs without changing the code. EU companies must have an EUID for communication between registers; they continue to use the domestic registration number in their own communications. FATF INR 24 includes a unique identifier such as a tax identification number in the company-registry basic set. A date is not an identifier.

questions.text: What identifier did the authoritative formation or licensing register assign, and which GLEIF Registration Authority code identifies that register?
Does the entity have an ISO 17442 LEI, an EU EUID, and/or other governed identifiers, and which is used for which interoperability plane?
Has uniqueness been preserved (one LEI per entity), and if the LEI was ported, which LOU now maintains it without changing the code?
If no authoritative register or LEI identifier exists yet, which UUID or ULID has the adopting Dimension assigned as a provisional key?

data_elements.name: Registration authority entity ID
data_elements.description: The identifier of the legal entity in the business registry or other registration authority of the jurisdiction of legal registration.

data_elements.name: Legal Entity Identifier
data_elements.description: 20-character ISO 17442 LEI with valid check digits.

data_elements.name: European unique identifier
data_elements.description: EUID used to identify the company unequivocally in BRIS communications between registers.

data_elements.name: Other unique identifier
data_elements.description: Additional unique identifier recorded by the company registry, such as a tax identification number or equivalent under FATF INR 24 paragraph 4(a).

data_elements.name: Dimension-assigned identifier
data_elements.description: UUID or ULID assigned by the adopting Dimension when no master or governed global identifier is yet available.

artifacts.name: LEI Data Record
artifacts.description: GLEIS Level 1 record for the entity, including LEI, entity block and registration block.
artifacts.identity_strategy: The LEI itself is the record key; last-update timestamp is metadata, not an identifier.

bundles.name: Jurisdiction and legal form
bundles.description: The law that constitutes the entity and the jurisdiction-specific legal form through which personality is taken. Legal form is not a global taxonomy of equivalent company types.
bundles.rationale: ISO 20275 assigns a unique ELF code per legal form per jurisdiction and explicitly does not align similarly named forms across countries. GLEIF and ISO 17442 treat legal jurisdiction and legal form as mandatory identification attributes. EU disclosure always includes legal form.

layers.name: Governing jurisdiction of formation
layers.description: The legal system under which the entity is formed, usually implied by the legal form and the register that constituted it.

findings.name: Legal jurisdiction of formation
findings.description: GLEIF Level 1 records LegalJurisdiction as the jurisdiction of legal formation, with country and subdivision coded in the ISO 3166 series. ISO 20275 commentary used by GLEIF states that legal form determines legal jurisdiction. FATF INR 24 applies to legal persons created in the country and to foreign-created legal persons that present ML/TF risks and have sufficient links. EU disclosure includes the Member State where the company is registered.

questions.text: Which legal jurisdiction constituted this entity, at country and, where relevant, subnational level?
If the entity was created abroad, does this operating jurisdiction assert sufficient FATF links requiring basic or beneficial-ownership information to be available here?
Which law governs internal affairs, and is the registered office required to be in that same jurisdiction?

data_elements.name: Legal jurisdiction
data_elements.description: Jurisdiction of legal formation, typically an ISO 3166 country or subdivision code as used in LEI-CDF LegalJurisdiction.

data_elements.name: Created in reporting country
data_elements.description: Whether the entity was created in the country whose transparency rules are being applied (FATF INR 24 paragraph 1).

data_elements.name: Sufficient links flag
data_elements.description: Whether a foreign-created legal person has sufficient links to the reporting country for Recommendation 24 duties.

findings.inline_only_rationale: Jurisdiction is coded reference data on the registration record, aligned to ISO 3166 and the GLEIF accepted legal-jurisdictions list. Supporting artefacts are the constituting instrument and register file, not a separate jurisdiction document.

layers.name: Entity legal form
layers.description: The distinct legal form in a jurisdiction, coded without cross-country equivalence.

findings.name: Entity legal form classification
findings.description: ISO 20275 specifies an unambiguous scheme to identify distinct entity legal forms in a jurisdiction so they can be classified. The ELF code is four Basic Latin characters, contains no embedded intelligence, and is unique per form per jurisdiction: a Limited Liability Company in one country must not reuse another country's code even if the names look similar. GLEIF's February 2026 list covers more than 3,600 forms in more than 200 jurisdictions, in native-language labels (Ltd, GmbH, SA and others). EU disclosure always includes legal form. OtherLegalForm is used in LEI-CDF when no ELF code applies.

questions.text: What ISO 20275 ELF code and native-language legal-form label apply in the formation jurisdiction?
Has any mapping claimed that this legal form is equivalent to a form in another jurisdiction, and is that mapping marked as non-normative?
If no ELF code exists, what OtherLegalForm text is recorded and has a code-list gap been raised with the maintenance agency?

data_elements.name: Entity legal form code
data_elements.description: Four-character ISO 20275 ELF code assigned to this jurisdiction's legal form.

data_elements.name: Legal form local name
data_elements.description: Legal form designation in the official or native language of the jurisdiction.

data_elements.name: Other legal form
data_elements.description: Free-text legal form used when no ELF code is assigned.

artifacts.name: ELF code-list entry
artifacts.description: Published GLEIF/ISO 20275 code-list row for the form, including jurisdiction and native-language label.
artifacts.identity_strategy: ELF code plus jurisdiction of the form, as published in a dated code-list version.

bundles.name: Registers, constituting instruments and representatives
bundles.description: The authoritative register or other registration authority, the company file, constituting documents, persons authorised to bind the entity, and the legal-owner or member register required as basic information.
bundles.rationale: GLEIF requires a cross-reference to a local authoritative source via the Registration Authorities List. FATF requires every company created in a country to be registered in a company registry that records a defined basic set. EU law opens a file in a central, commercial or companies register and mandates disclosure of statutes, officers and capital particulars. UNCITRAL makes registration constitutive for the LLE.

layers.name: Registration authorities and register files
layers.description: Which body maintains the authoritative record and how that body is coded for interoperability.

findings.name: Authoritative register binding
findings.description: GLEIF publishes codes for more than 1,050 business registers and other validation sources in 232 jurisdictions. LEI issuers must populate RegistrationAuthorityID and ValidationAuthorityID from that list; reserved codes include RA777777 PUBLIC LEGAL DOCUMENT for general government entities and international organisations not in a regular register, plus RA888888 and RA999999. FATF defines a company registry as a register in the country of companies incorporated or licensed there, normally maintained by or for the incorporating authority, not information held only by the company. EU Member States open a file in a central, commercial or companies register for each registered company.

questions.text: Which registration authority is the authoritative source for this entity, and what GLEIF RA code identifies it?
answer_data: code register_kind (companies, commercial, central, licensing, public-legal-document, other)

questions.text: Is a reserved RA code in use because no ordinary register exists, and what public legal document or exception justifies it?
If the validation authority differs from the registration authority, which authority corroborated the record and to what level?
Has a company file been opened in the register, and what is the file or registration number used for filings and disclosure?

data_elements.name: Registration authority ID
data_elements.description: GLEIF Registration Authorities List code for the business register or other registration authority.

data_elements.name: Validation authority ID
data_elements.description: GLEIF RA code of the authority used to corroborate the record, which may differ from the registration authority.

data_elements.name: Register kind
data_elements.description: Whether the source is a companies, commercial or central register, a licensing or fund authority, or a public legal document.

artifacts.name: Company or legal-entity register file
artifacts.description: The file opened in the central, commercial or companies register, or equivalent authoritative source, holding disclosed documents and particulars.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Registration authority code plus register entity ID / file number; EUID when communicating between EU registers.

findings.name: EUID and register interconnection
findings.description: EU companies must have an EUID allowing unequivocal identification in communications between registers through BRIS, which comprises Member State registers, a European central platform and the e-Justice portal. The platform must not store a centralised companies database of substantive information, must not alter domestic register content, and uses unique identifiers to distribute information. BRIS messages include EUID and Alternate ID such as LEI, and support branch disclosure and other cross-border notifications. Domestic registration numbers remain the numbers companies use in their own letters.

questions.text: What is the company's EUID, and which country code, register identifier and domestic number compose it?
Which alternate identifiers, including any LEI, are attached to BRIS notifications for this company?
Which BRIS notifications (branch disclosure, cross-border merger or other) have been sent or received for this entity, and when?
answer_data: collection bris_notifications {type, direction, counterpart_register, timestamp event_time, timestamp observed_at}

data_elements.name: BRIS participant flag
data_elements.description: Whether the entity is in scope of the EU system of interconnection of registers.

data_elements.name: Alternate register identifiers
data_elements.description: Other identifiers carried in BRIS messages, for example LEI.

artifacts.name: BRIS interchange notification
artifacts.description: Electronic notification exchanged between the register of the company and the register of a branch or other connected register.
artifacts.identity_strategy: EUID of the company plus notification type and event time; observation/ingestion time recorded separately.

layers.name: Constituting instruments, officers and legal owners
layers.description: Documents that create and regulate the entity, the persons who can bind it, and the legal-owner register FATF treats as basic information.

findings.name: Constituting instruments and disclosed particulars
findings.description: EU Article 14 requires compulsory disclosure of the instrument of constitution and statutes, subsequent amendments, persons authorised to bind the company, capital particulars, accounting documents required to be published, change of registered office, winding-up, judicial declaration of nullity, appointment of liquidators and termination of liquidation. Articles 3 and 4 require type and name, objects, capital and duration in the statutes, and registered office in the statutes or a disclosed document. FATF INR 24 paragraph 4(a) requires company name, proof of incorporation, legal form and status, registered-office address, basic regulating powers (for example memorandum and articles), a list of directors, and a unique identifier. UNCITRAL LLE Recommendation 9 limits formation information to the minimum needed for operation and third-party protection, including name, address or geographic location, and identity of the applicant and of persons managing the business. The Guide does not require organisation rules to be public.

questions.text: Which constituting instruments (instrument of constitution, statutes, articles, organisation rules) are on the register file, in which language and at which version?
answer_data: collection instruments {type, identifier, language, version, timestamp filed_at, timestamp effective_at}

questions.text: What objects, capital (authorised and subscribed) and duration does the constituting instrument state?
Which directors, legal representatives or designated managers are disclosed as authorised to bind the entity, and what are their powers and appointment interval?
answer_data: collection representatives {role, person_or_entity_ref, powers, timestamp appointed_at, timestamp ceased_at, boolean nominee_flag}

questions.text: Does the company keep a register of shareholders or members (names, shares or interests, classes and voting rights), and is it held at the registered office, another notified location, or only abroad because beneficial-ownership information is held in-country?
answer_data: collection legal_owners {name, identifier, interest_amount, class, voting_rights}

data_elements.name: Objects clause
data_elements.description: Stated objects or purpose of the company in the constituting instrument.

data_elements.name: Subscribed capital
data_elements.description: Amount of capital subscribed, as disclosed under EU company law where applicable.

data_elements.name: Disclosed representatives
data_elements.description: Persons authorised to bind the company, directors, or UNCITRAL designated managers recorded on the register.

data_elements.name: Legal-owner register location
data_elements.description: Where the shareholder or member register required by FATF INR 24 paragraph 4(b) is maintained.

artifacts.name: Statutes, articles or instrument of constitution
artifacts.description: The instrument of constitution and statutes or articles of association, including a complete text after each amendment.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register document number plus version/effective date; hash of the filed binary for integrity.

artifacts.name: Directors and representatives filing
artifacts.description: Appointment, termination and particulars of persons authorised to bind the company.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Filing number on the company file plus role and person reference; dates are validity, not identity.

bundles.name: Seat, addresses and establishments
bundles.description: The legal seat, registered office, address of legal formation, headquarters, and registered branches or other establishments through which the entity is present in a territory.
bundles.rationale: ISO 17442 and GLEIF require the address of legal formation and the headquarters address. EU law treats registered office as compulsory information and requires disclosure of any change. Branches have their own disclosure and interconnection duties and, in the EU, their own unique identifier for register communications.

layers.name: Registered office and legal address
layers.description: The address that the law treats as the entity's seat for service, disclosure and connecting factors.

findings.name: Registered office and legal address of formation
findings.description: GLEIF Level 1 separates LegalAddress (address of legal formation) from HeadquartersAddress. EU Article 4 requires the registered office to appear in the statutes or a disclosed document; Article 14 requires disclosure of any change of registered office; free BRIS information includes the registered office and Member State of registration. UNCITRAL Recommendation 9 requires the address at which the business is deemed to receive correspondence, or a precise geographic location if there is no standard-form address. Residential addresses of managers are not required for LLE formation.

questions.text: What is the registered office or legal address of formation, including country and subdivision, and is it the address for service?
What is the headquarters address if different from the legal address, and in which language was the source address recorded?
When did a change of registered office become effective in the formation jurisdiction, and when was it disclosed on the register?

data_elements.name: Legal address
data_elements.description: Address of legal formation or registered office as structured address data.

data_elements.name: Headquarters address
data_elements.description: Address of the headquarters of the legal entity or international branch.

data_elements.name: Address for service
data_elements.description: Address at which the entity is deemed to receive correspondence, including a geographic-location description when no standard-form address exists.

artifacts.name: Registered-office disclosure
artifacts.description: Filing or register extract stating the registered office and subsequent changes.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Company file number plus filing identifier; effective date of the seat change is event time, not the artefact identifier.

layers.name: Branches and establishments
layers.description: Registered presence that is not a separately incorporated subsidiary.

findings.name: Registered branches and international establishments
findings.description: EU law treats the opening of a branch as an establishment option distinct from creating a subsidiary. The host-State register must disclose branch particulars and refer to the register of the company; letters of the branch must state the register in which the branch is entered. Branches of a dissolved company must be struck off without undue delay. ISO 17442-1:2020 explicitly includes international branches as eligible legal entities for an LEI even though company law may not treat them as separate legal persons. BRIS exchanges branch disclosure notifications using the company's EUID. Third-country branches in comparable legal forms are also covered by the Directive with specific provisions.

questions.text: Which branches or international establishments are registered, in which host registers, and under which host identifiers?
answer_data: collection branches {host_jurisdiction, host_register_id, host_entity_id, euid_if_any, lei_if_any, status}

questions.text: Does the host or home law treat this establishment as a separate legal person, an international branch eligible for its own LEI, or only a register object of the parent company?
If the company was dissolved or wound up, has each registered branch been struck off without undue delay, and at what event time?
answer_data: collection branch_strike_offs {branch_id, timestamp struck_off_at, timestamp observed_at}

data_elements.name: Branch records
data_elements.description: Registered branches or international establishments linked to the company.

data_elements.name: Parent company reference
data_elements.description: Home-register identifier of the company of which the branch is part.

artifacts.name: Branch register extract
artifacts.description: Host-register disclosure for the branch, including reference to the company's home register.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Host register identifier plus branch registration number; company EUID as the linking key in BRIS.

bundles.name: Lifecycle, status and legal-entity events
bundles.description: How the legal person comes into existence, which status it currently has, which events change its identity or existence, and how insolvency, merger, conversion, nullity and expiration are recorded on the register.
bundles.rationale: GLEIF distinguishes EntityStatus (whether the entity is legally registered and operating) from RegistrationStatus of the LEI record. EU law requires disclosure of winding-up, nullity and liquidators. UNCITRAL makes registration constitutive, reserves conversion, restructuring and dissolution to members, and treats liquidation of a legal entity as typically ending in dissolution. Dates of creation, first LEI assignment, last update and event effectivity are first-class ISO 17442 attributes.

layers.name: Formation, status and expiration
layers.description: Birth, current legal status and end of legal existence.

findings.name: Formation and creation
findings.description: UNCITRAL Recommendation 8: the LLE is formed once it is registered. Recommendation 2 allows formation for any lawful business or commercial activity. ISO 17442 and GLEIF record EntityCreationDate as the date the entity was first established (ISO 8601), plus InitialRegistrationDate of the LEI (first assignment/publication) and LastUpdateDate of the data record. Event time in the formation jurisdiction must be stored separately from observation or ingestion time. Online EU formation and filing procedures exist as an overlay on national registers, not as a substitute for the register file.

questions.text: On what date and time, with which offset, was the entity first established in the formation jurisdiction?
When was the LEI or national registration first assigned or published, and when was this data record last updated and why?
Was the entity formed through an online procedure, paper filing, statutory instrument or public legal document, and who submitted the application?

data_elements.name: Entity creation date-time
data_elements.description: Date and time the legal entity was first established, with timezone, as in LEI-CDF EntityCreationDate.

data_elements.name: Initial identifier registration date-time
data_elements.description: Date of first assignment or publication of the LEI or equivalent identifier record.

data_elements.name: Last update date-time
data_elements.description: Date and time the identifier data record was last updated, with reason.

data_elements.name: Formation channel
data_elements.description: Online, paper, statutory or public-legal-document channel used to form the entity.

artifacts.name: Formation application and registration notice
artifacts.description: Application, supporting identity evidence of the submitter, and the register's notice that the entity is formed.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Register-assigned application or filing number; creation timestamp is event metadata.

findings.name: Status, dissolution, expiration and nullity
findings.description: GLEIF EntityStatus is ACTIVE if the entity reported it was legally registered and operating; INACTIVE if it is no longer legally registered and/or operating because of closure, acquisition/merger or illegitimacy; NULL when not applicable. EntityExpirationDate and EntityExpirationReason (dissolved, corporate action, other) record cessation. LEI RegistrationStatus (ISSUED, LAPSED, RETIRED and others) describes the identifier record, not the legal person: completed liquidation or insolvency events shall move RegistrationStatus to RETIRED. EU Article 14 requires disclosure of winding-up, judicial nullity and liquidators. UNCITRAL members reserve decisions on dissolution; insolvency guidance states liquidation of a commercial legal entity usually results in dissolution. Restoration after administrative strike-off is a known national lifecycle that is not specified in the fetched global instruments and is recorded as a gap.

questions.text: What is the legal-entity status, what is the identifier registration status, and are they being kept distinct?
If the entity ceased to exist or operate, what is the expiration date-time, the expiration reason, and the successor if any?
Has winding-up, a judicial declaration of nullity, or appointment of liquidators been disclosed, and what powers do the liquidators have?
Has a completed liquidation or insolvency event required the LEI RegistrationStatus to become RETIRED while still allowing quality amendments?

data_elements.name: Entity status
data_elements.description: ACTIVE, INACTIVE or NULL as defined by LEI-CDF EntityStatusEnum.

data_elements.name: Identifier registration status
data_elements.description: Status of the LEI or equivalent identifier record (for example ISSUED, LAPSED, RETIRED), which must not be treated as entity status.

data_elements.name: Entity expiration date-time
data_elements.description: Date and time the entity ceased to exist and/or operate.

data_elements.name: Entity expiration reason
data_elements.description: Reason the entity ceased: dissolved, corporate action, or other.

data_elements.name: Successor entity
data_elements.description: Entity that succeeded this one after merger, absorption or similar corporate action.

artifacts.name: Winding-up, liquidation or nullity filing
artifacts.description: Disclosed winding-up, appointment of liquidators, termination of liquidation, striking off, or judicial declaration of nullity.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuing court or register document number; event effective time stored separately from filing time.

layers.name: Legal-entity events and succession
layers.description: Events that change reference data or legal existence, with an effective date in the formation jurisdiction.

findings.name: Legal-entity events, mergers and conversion
findings.description: ISO 17442 and GLEIF CDF 3.1 add the effective date of a legal-entity event in the jurisdiction of formation. GLEIF business rules require specified completed events such as liquidation and insolvency to retire the LEI record, while other events keep ISSUED or LAPSED status. UNCITRAL reserves conversion, restructuring and dissolution to members and expects those decisions to be recorded. EU BRIS supports cross-border merger information exchange between registers. Successor-entity linkage is part of Level 1 reference data after corporate actions.

questions.text: Which legal-entity events are recorded, with which type, status, effective time in the formation jurisdiction, and observation time?
answer_data: collection events {type, status, timestamp effective_at, timestamp observed_at, text description, identifier evidence_id}

questions.text: Which predecessor and successor legal persons are linked by merger, absorption, spin-off, conversion or restructuring, and which identifiers survived?
answer_data: collection related_entities {relation, identifier, scheme, timestamp effective_at}

questions.text: Was conversion, restructuring or dissolution decided by the members (or competent court) as required, and is that decision on the register file?

data_elements.name: Legal-entity events
data_elements.description: Structured events affecting the entity, each with type, status and effective timestamp in the formation jurisdiction.

data_elements.name: Event effective at
data_elements.description: Date and time the event was effective in the legal jurisdiction of formation.

artifacts.name: Event supporting instrument
artifacts.description: Merger plan, conversion resolution, court order or register notice that evidences a legal-entity event.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuing body document identifier plus event type; effective time is not the identifier.

bundles.name: Transparency, validation, access and retention
bundles.description: How register data is corroborated, who may access basic and beneficial-ownership information, which obstacles to transparency are forbidden, and how long records are kept after the entity ends.
bundles.rationale: GLEIF separates entity-supplied, partially corroborated and fully corroborated validation. FATF Recommendation 24 and INR 24 impose a multi-pronged beneficial-ownership regime, public basic information, competent-authority access, bearer-share and nominee controls, and five-year retention after dissolution. EU law makes specified particulars free through BRIS and allows third parties to rely on disclosed documents.

layers.name: Corroboration and data quality
layers.description: Evidence that reference data matches the local authoritative source.

findings.name: Corroboration and validation sources
findings.description: ISO 17442 requires the status of validation, publication and updating of the LEI and supporting data. GLEIF records ValidationSources and a ValidationAuthority drawn from the Registration Authorities List. Cross-reference to the local authoritative source is mandatory when a specific RA code exists. Recipients of LEI-CDF files must ignore unknown extensions and still interpret standard content. Historical and current records are published in the Global LEI Index.

questions.text: Against which validation authority and at which validation-sources level was this record corroborated?
Which data-quality issues, challenges or lapsed-renewal states are open on this record, and who raised them?
answer_data: collection quality_flags {code, text, identifier raised_by, timestamp raised_at, code status}

questions.text: Do any publisher extensions exist, and can the standard identification content be interpreted if they are ignored?

data_elements.name: Validation sources
data_elements.description: GLEIF indication of whether data is pending, entity-supplied only, partially corroborated or fully corroborated.

data_elements.name: Next renewal date
data_elements.description: Date by which an LEI registration must be renewed to avoid lapse.

data_elements.name: Quality flags
data_elements.description: Open data-quality issues or challenge outcomes on the registration record.

artifacts.name: Corroboration evidence pack
artifacts.description: Extract or public legal document used to corroborate the legal name, form, address and identifier against the local authoritative source.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Validation-authority identifier plus evidence document number and hash; not the corroboration date.

layers.name: Access, retention and obstacles to transparency
layers.description: Who may see which layer of information, for how long, and which anonymity devices are forbidden.

findings.name: Basic information and beneficial-ownership duties
findings.description: FATF INR 24 requires all companies created in a country to be registered. The company registry must record the paragraph 4(a) basic set and make it public. Companies must obtain and hold adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial-ownership information and cooperate with competent authorities. Countries must use a multi-pronged approach: the company itself plus a public authority or body (tax authority, FIU, company registry or beneficial-ownership registry) or a documented alternative mechanism that is not mere reuse of basic information. Competent authorities must have timely access; countries should require the company registry to facilitate access by financial institutions, DNFBPs and foreign competent authorities to public basic information, should consider access to the shareholder register and beneficial-ownership information, and could consider public access to beneficial-ownership information. Public procurement authorities need timely access. This finding records the duty, holding body and access posture; it does not store the beneficial-ownership graph.

questions.text: Is the FATF paragraph 4(a) basic set complete on the company registry and available as public information?
Which prongs of the multi-pronged approach are in use, and which public authority or alternative mechanism holds beneficial-ownership information?
Who may access basic information, the legal-owner register, and beneficial-ownership information, under which legal basis, and are there privacy or security exceptions?
answer_data: collection access_rules {layer, principal_class, legal_basis, boolean public}

questions.text: Does the entity have existing bearer shares or nominee shareholders or directors, and which mitigation measures apply given that new bearer shares must not be issued?

data_elements.name: Basic information public
data_elements.description: Whether FATF INR 24 paragraph 4(a) basic information is publicly available via the company registry.

data_elements.name: Beneficial-ownership holding body type
data_elements.description: Public authority or body type holding BO information, or an alternative mechanism.

data_elements.name: Existing bearer shares present
data_elements.description: Whether existing bearer shares or warrants remain, even though new issues are forbidden.

data_elements.name: Nominee arrangements present
data_elements.description: Whether nominee shareholders or directors are recorded, requiring FATF mitigation measures.

artifacts.name: Beneficial-ownership filing pointer
artifacts.description: Pointer to the BO return or registry record that satisfies the legal-person transparency duty, without embedding the ownership graph in this model.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Holding-body identifier plus their master BO record identifier; this model stores the pointer, not the graph.

findings.name: Retention, disclosure and third-party reliance
findings.description: FATF INR 24 paragraph 8 requires companies, administrators, liquidators and the authorities and entities that hold basic or beneficial-ownership information to keep it for at least five years after the company is dissolved or otherwise ceases to exist, or five years after it ceases to be a customer of an intermediary or financial institution. EU law makes electronic copies available through BRIS; specified particulars are free of charge (name and legal form, registered office, Member State, registration number, and later representatives, branches, status and object). Third parties may rely on disclosed documents and on voluntary translations unless they knew of the authentic version. Registers typically keep historical legal-identity records beyond AML retention for legal certainty; hard deletion of a registration history is exceptional.

questions.text: When did the five-year FATF retention clock start (dissolution, cessation of existence, or end of customer relationship), and is a longer legal-certainty archive also in force?
Which particulars are available free of charge through the register or BRIS, and which copies may be charged only at administrative cost?
May third parties rely on the disclosed instruments and translations, and are there known discrepancies between authentic and translated versions?

data_elements.name: Retention start at
data_elements.description: Event time from which the minimum five-year FATF retention runs.

data_elements.name: Minimum retention
data_elements.description: Minimum retention duration after dissolution or cessation; FATF specifies at least five years.

data_elements.name: Third-party reliance
data_elements.description: Whether disclosed register particulars may be relied on by third parties under the applicable company-law disclosure rules.

artifacts.name: Certified register copy
artifacts.description: Electronic or paper copy of disclosed documents issued by the register, including any certified translation.
artifacts.identity_strategy: Issuing register identifier plus copy/certification number; certification time is provenance, not identity.

functions.name: Form and register a legal entity
functions.description: Accept a formation application, verify minimum particulars, open a register file and, in constitutive-registration systems, bring the legal person into existence.
inputs: proposed name, legal form, jurisdiction, address and representatives
outputs: proof of incorporation or registration notice
preconditions: Proposed activity is lawful in the formation jurisdiction.
Legal form is one recognised in that jurisdiction.
Name clears public-policy and collision rules where required.
effects: A company file exists in the authoritative register.
In constitutive systems, legal personality attaches at registration.
Basic information required by FATF INR 24 paragraph 4(a) is recorded.

functions.name: Bind authoritative and global identifiers
functions.description: Attach the register-assigned master identifier and, where eligible, issue or link an LEI and, in the EU, an EUID, preserving one LEI per entity.
preconditions: Authoritative register identity exists or is created in the same transaction.
No conflicting live LEI already uniquely identifies the same legal entity.
effects: The record can be addressed by master-system, governed-global and Dimension identifiers in the required priority.
Porting an LEI later must not change the code.

functions.name: Update register particulars
functions.description: File and publish changes to name, registered office, representatives, capital, objects, legal form or other disclosed particulars, with event-effective time distinct from filing time.
preconditions: Filer is a person authorised to bind the entity or a competent authority or liquidator.
Entity has not been finally dissolved unless the update is a quality or winding-up amendment.
effects: Disclosed record matches the new legal facts from the event effective time.
Third-party reliance follows the disclosure rules of the jurisdiction.

functions.name: Corroborate reference data against the authoritative source
functions.description: Compare Level 1 or Dimension reference data with the local register or public legal document and set validation sources and quality flags.
inputs: source extract or public legal document
preconditions: A specific RA code exists, or a reserved code such as RA777777 is justified.
effects: Record is marked entity-supplied, partially corroborated or fully corroborated.
Unknown CDF extensions are ignored without rejecting the standard content.

functions.name: Record a legal-entity event
functions.description: Capture merger, conversion, name or seat change, insolvency, liquidation, dissolution or similar events with jurisdiction-effective time and successor links.
preconditions: Event is effective under the formation-jurisdiction law.
Required member, court or registrar decision exists for structural events.
effects: Completed liquidation or insolvency retires the LEI registration status where GLEIF rules apply.

functions.name: Disclose and interconnect register data
functions.description: Make compulsory particulars available nationally and, where applicable, through BRIS or the Global LEI Index, including branch notifications and free basic information.
preconditions: Document is in the compulsory disclosure set or the entity has opted to disclose it.
effects: Specified particulars are free through BRIS where EU law applies.
EUID and alternate IDs travel in cross-register messages without creating a central companies database.

functions.name: Enforce transparency duties and retention
functions.description: Ensure basic information is public, beneficial-ownership information is held under a multi-pronged approach, bearer-share and nominee risks are mitigated, and records are kept at least five years after dissolution.
preconditions: The subject is a legal person created in the country or a foreign legal person with sufficient links.
effects: Competent authorities can obtain adequate, accurate and up-to-date information rapidly.
Minimum retention survives dissolution; legal-certainty archives may last longer. Hard deletion of identity history remains exceptional.

composition.purpose: This registration record is the legal-person facet of an organisation; the parent holds social and operational identity that may exist with or without legal personality.
Align eligible-party definition, minimum identification attributes and the optional global identifier; do not treat LEI as a substitute for the incorporating-register master identifier.
Classify jurisdiction-specific legal forms without asserting cross-country equivalence.
Align EU register-file, EUID, disclosure, branch and interconnection rules as a regional profile, not a global default.

Align company-registry basic information, multi-pronged beneficial-ownership holding, access, bearer-share/nominee constraints and five-year retention, without absorbing the beneficial-ownership graph.
Point to the sibling model that stores natural-person control and ownership percentages; this model stores only the duty, holding body, pointer, access and quality.
Keep trusts and similar legal arrangements out of this legal-person model unless a jurisdiction registers them as legal persons.
Consume insolvency and liquidation outcomes as register-visible events and status transitions without modelling the estate or creditor process.

composition.target: Natural person and official organisational role
composition.purpose: Link disclosed directors, managers, applicants and legal owners to person/role masters rather than duplicating biographical data.
Reuse structured address geometry and service-of-process semantics for legal address, registered office and headquarters.
Reuse a tax identification number when the company registry records it as a unique identifier, without importing tax assessment.
Treat vLEI credentials as a digital projection of an already registered legal-entity identity chained to GLEIF as root of trust, not as a substitute for the register.

owner_package_requirements: Declare the formation jurisdiction, authoritative registration-authority code and master register identifier before asserting a legal-entity record as canonical.
Keep entity status distinct from identifier-registration status, and keep event-effective time distinct from observation or ingestion time.
Do not treat ELF codes, national company numbers or LEIs as interchangeable keys; record scheme, issuing authority and purpose for every identifier.
Package constituting instruments, register extracts and corroboration evidence as serial artefacts with integrity hashes rather than as unversioned blobs.
dimension.namespace_guidance: Use a jurisdiction-qualified namespace for register-native identifiers (registration-authority code + entity ID) and the GLEIF LEI namespace for ISO 17442 codes. Dimension-assigned UUIDs or ULIDs live in the adopting Dimension namespace and must be marked provisional until bound to a master register identifier or LEI. Do not mint a new LEI-shaped or EUID-shaped string.
registry_links: GLEIF Accepted Legal Jurisdictions Code List
EU Business Registers Interconnection System / e-Justice portal
National central, commercial or companies registers identified by RA code

canonicalization_rules: Canonical legal name is the register or constituting-instrument name in its original language; transliterations and trading names are aliases, not replacements.
Canonical jurisdiction is the legal jurisdiction of formation implied by legal form and constituting register, coded to ISO 3166.
Canonical identifier priority: incorporating-register master ID; then LEI and/or EUID; then Dimension UUID/ULID. Dates are never identifiers.
ELF codes are canonical only with their jurisdiction of form; never merge two ELF codes because English labels look similar.
Append-only event history; corrections are patches with provenance, not silent overwrites of effective-time facts.
patch_rules: Patches to name, address, representatives or form must carry the legal-entity event effective time and the filing or observation time.
Identifier patches may bind a provisional Dimension ID to a later-issued register ID or LEI but must not recycle a retired LEI onto a different legal person.
Quality amendments after LEI retirement are allowed only to remediate data-quality issues or code-list updates, not to resurrect a dissolved person.
BO-graph updates patch the sibling model; this model patches only the holding-body pointer, access rule and quality of the duty.
compatibility_rules: A record without an LEI remains valid if it has an authoritative register identifier.
A record with an LEI but a lapsed RegistrationStatus remains a valid identification of an ACTIVE or INACTIVE legal person.
EU EUID compatibility is required only for BRIS-participating companies and branches.
Consumers must ignore unknown extensions in identifier payloads (LEI-CDF rule) without rejecting the standard content.
Non-equivalence of ELF codes across jurisdictions is a compatibility invariant.

identity_priority: Authoritative master-system identifier: Document or file number assigned by the authoritative register or court.
Governed global identifier of the entity to which the artefact belongs (LEI or EUID) plus artefact type and version.
SHA-256 or stronger hash of the stored binary, used as integrity key, with a Dimension ULID only when the issuer provided no document number.
artifact_rules.timestamp_rule: All event, filing, certification, corroboration and ingestion times use RFC 3339 with seconds and an explicit offset or Z; store legal-effect time in the formation jurisdiction separately from observation or ingestion time.
artifact_rules.serial_naming_rule: Serial artefacts use {ra-code-or-issuer}/{entity-id}/{artefact-type}/v{n}-{effective-date} where v{n} increments on each filed version; never encode meaning in the identifier beyond issuer, entity, type and version.
artifact_rules.integrity_rule: Each stored artefact carries a cryptographic hash and the issuing-authority identifier; certified copies reference the hash of the authentic version they reproduce, and translations reference the authentic-language original.

policies: One legally distinct entity receives at most one live LEI; porting changes the managing LOU, not the code.
National register identifiers remain authoritative in the formation jurisdiction even when an LEI or EUID exists.
EntityStatus and identifier RegistrationStatus must never be collapsed into a single status field.
New bearer shares or bearer share warrants must not be issued; existing instruments and nominee arrangements require recorded mitigations.

Minimum retention of basic and beneficial-ownership information is five years after dissolution or cessation; legal-identity history should not be hard-deleted while third-party reliance or restoration remains possible.
Public access applies to the FATF basic set and to EU free BRIS particulars; beneficial-ownership access follows the jurisdiction's documented multi-pronged choice and privacy exceptions.

read: Anyone may read public basic information and free BRIS/LEI Index particulars without creating an account.
Financial institutions, DNFBPs and foreign competent authorities receive facilitated access to public company-registry information.
Competent authorities and public-procurement authorities receive timely access to basic and beneficial-ownership information under FATF INR 24.
Certified copies and charged documents are issued against the register's fee and identity rules.
create: Formation filings create a register file and, where constitutive, legal personality.
LEI issuance is performed only by an accredited LOU against corroborated Level 1 data.
Dimension create of a provisional record is allowed only with a declared jurisdiction and a plan to bind a master identifier.
Creating a second live LEI for the same legal person is forbidden.
update: Authorised representatives, liquidators or the registrar may update disclosed particulars and legal-entity events.
LOUs update LEI reference data and may receive ported records.
Quality challenges may update flags without changing legal-effect history.
Structural updates (conversion, merger, dissolution) require the decision instrument on file.
delete: Do not hard-delete a legal-entity identity record. Strike-off, retirement, annulment or dissolution are status transitions with retention.
After the FATF minimum retention and any longer legal-certainty period, artefacts may be archived or redacted according to the register's law; the identifier and status history remain.
Duplicate or fraudulently issued identifier records may be marked DUPLICATE or ANNULLED rather than erased.
Provisional Dimension IDs that were never bound may be withdrawn with an audit reason.

roles.name: Registration authority / registrar
responsibilities: Open and maintain the company or legal-entity file.
Assign the master register identifier and, where applicable, the EUID.
Disclose compulsory particulars and issue certified copies.
Exchange BRIS or equivalent cross-register notifications.

roles.name: Legal entity (filing subject)
responsibilities: Keep disclosed particulars and the legal-owner register accurate.
Obtain and hold adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial-ownership information and cooperate with competent authorities.
File legal-entity events, including winding-up and representative changes.

roles.name: LEI issuing organization (LOU)
responsibilities: Issue, renew, port and retire LEIs against GLEIF/ROC rules.
Corroborate Level 1 data to the local authoritative source.
Publish CDF-conformant records without making extensions mandatory for consumers.

roles.name: Competent authority
responsibilities: Obtain timely access to basic and beneficial-ownership information.
Assess misuse risk of legal persons, including foreign-created persons with sufficient links.
Use register data in supervision, investigation, public procurement and international cooperation.

roles.name: Relying third party
responsibilities: Rely on disclosed register particulars within the jurisdiction's publicity rules.
Treat translations as non-authentic unless the company cannot prove knowledge of the authentic version.
Use LEI or EUID only as identification aids, not as proof of capacity beyond the supporting register data.

roles.name: Dimension data steward
responsibilities: Enforce identifier priority, RFC 3339 timestamps and append-only event history.
Bind provisional Dimension IDs to master identifiers.
Keep this model from absorbing sibling BO, insolvency, tax and person graphs.

access.default_rule: Public read of FATF basic information and EU free BRIS/LEI Index particulars; authenticated and authorised read of non-public legal-owner and beneficial-ownership layers; write only by the registrar, the entity's authorised filers, liquidators, accredited LOUs and Dimension stewards within their scope.
exceptions: Competent-authority and FIU access overrides public-access limitations on beneficial-ownership and legal-owner data.
Privacy and data-protection rules may restrict public BO access even where basic information remains public; record the legal basis rather than deleting the duty.
Sealed court files, sanctions-related redactions and identity-protection orders may withhold representative particulars while preserving the fact of an order.
RA777777 public-legal-document sources may be public as law yet lack a queryable register API.
audit_requirements: Log every create, update, status transition, disclosure, certified-copy issuance and access to non-public layers with actor, scope, purpose, event time and ingestion time.
Retain audit logs at least as long as the underlying legal-entity artefacts.
Record LEI challenge, port, lapse and retirement events with the managing LOU identifier.

read_order: Read AGENTS.md for Name, Type, Specification URL, Storage type URL, Interface URL and Processes URL before any create or update.
Read the specification (this model) to resolve identifier priority, jurisdiction, legal form and status semantics.
Read storage-type and interface contracts only as projections; do not infer legal meaning from JSON, YAML, MongoDB, Git or MCP shapes.
Read Processes URL for formation, event, disclosure, corroboration and retention workflows before executing them.

coverage.claim: This structure is a defensible, format-neutral context model for registered legal-person identity, jurisdiction, registers and lifecycle, grounded in ISO 17442/20275, GLEIF Level 1 and RA/ELF lists, EU company-law registers and BRIS, FATF Recommendation 24/INR 24 and UNCITRAL LLE formation rules. It is an alignment, not a worldwide companies code, and it deliberately stops at the boundary with organisation, beneficial-ownership graphs, legal arrangements, insolvency proceedings, tax and person masters.

checklist.notes: Master register identifier, LEI, EUID, FATF unique identifier such as TIN, Dimension UUID/ULID priority, official name and proof of incorporation.

Constitutive registration, entity versus identifier status, expiration reasons, winding-up, nullity, liquidation retirement of LEI, conversion and successor links. Restoration after strike-off is a documented gap.
Representatives, legal owners as basic information, branches, predecessor/successor, managing LOU, registration and validation authorities. Control percentages sit in a sibling.
Entity creation, identifier assignment, last update, event effective time versus observation/ingestion time, renewal date, RFC 3339 rule.
Validation sources, validation authority, corroboration evidence, CDF extensions ignored, LEI Index historical records.
Legal-owner/member register location and contents as FATF basic information; beneficial-ownership graph referenced, not stored.
Name collision, ELF code presence, RA-code corroboration, basic-set completeness, LEI check digits and uniqueness.
Public basic set, free BRIS particulars, competent-authority timely access, considered FI/DNFBP access, privacy exceptions.
FATF five-year post-dissolution retention; no hard delete of identity history; archive versus exceptional redaction.
LEI-CDF, BRIS/EUID, ELF and RA code lists, alternate IDs, vLEI as digital projection, non-equivalence of legal forms.
Distinct personality, capacity, limited liability, constitutive versus declaratory registration.
Legal jurisdiction of formation, sufficient links for foreign persons, ISO 20275 ELF without cross-country merge.
Company registry definition, GLEIF RA list including reserved public-legal-document code, EU register file.
Host-register disclosure, international-branch LEI eligibility versus non-personality, strike-off after dissolution.
Bearer shares forbidden for new issues; nominee shareholder and director mitigations required.

known_omissions: UNCITRAL Guide on Key Principles of a Business Registry (2018) is cited by the LLE Guide as the dedicated registry-operations instrument but was not independently fetched; operational registry-service design may be thinner than that Guide.
Administrative strike-off, restoration to the register, dormancy and administrative revival are nationally common and not specified in the fetched global instruments.

United States state secretaries of state, registered-agent statutes, China's Unified Social Credit Code, India's CIN and similar national identifier schemes are not modelled beyond the RA-list binding.
Full FATF INR 24 footnotes, verification methods and foreign-person 'sufficient links' tests are only partially extracted.
Digital-asset organisations, DAOs and other emerging personality experiments have no primary support in ISO 17442 eligibility as fetched.
Islamic waqf, cooperatives, unincorporated associations and mixed public-law bodies are covered only insofar as an ELF code or RA source exists.
EU proposal for an 'EU Inc.' 28th-regime corporate form (2026) is not in force and is excluded.
ISO 5009 official organisational roles and vLEI role credentials are alignment pointers, not a modelled officer ontology.
conflicts: The incorporating-register identifier is legally master in the formation jurisdiction; the LEI is a globally unique identifier for the same person but is not constitutive of personality.
EUID is mandatory for EU inter-register communication yet companies must continue to use domestic numbers in their own correspondence.
ISO 17442 includes individuals acting in a business capacity and international branches; many company registers and FATF 'legal persons' treatments do not treat those objects as companies.
ELF codes with similar English labels are not equivalent across jurisdictions; any crosswalk is heuristic and non-conformant to ISO 20275.
EntityStatus (legal existence/operation) and LEI RegistrationStatus (issued, lapsed, retired) can diverge and must not be fused.

FATF requires competent-authority access to beneficial-ownership information and only invites countries to consider public access; some regional regimes have made BO registers public and later restricted them. This model records the duty and the chosen access posture rather than claiming one global publicity rule.
UNCITRAL LLE is formed once registered (constitutive); some company-law systems treat registration as declaratory of a prior notarial constitution.
regional_assumptions: EU Directive 2017/1132, EUID and BRIS are a regional profile applied when the entity is an EU/EEA registered company or branch, not a global default.
GLEIF RA and ELF lists are globally broad (232 jurisdictions / 200+ jurisdictions) but still incomplete; absence from a list is a gap, not proof that no register or form exists.
Common-law registered-office-plus-registered-agent patterns and civil-law notarial constitutive deeds both map to the same address and instrument findings with different formation_theory codes.
FATF 'company registry' language is applied mutatis mutandis to other legal persons as INR 24 footnote 68 requires, without pretending every foundation or cooperative uses a companies house.
adversarial_checks: If a partnership or MSME has no legal personality, this model must refuse to mint a legal-person record even if a tax or licence number exists.
If two ELF codes share a name (LLC, SA) they must not be merged; doing so would violate ISO 20275's no-embedded-intelligence and no-cross-country-alignment rules.
If an LEI is lapsed or retired, identity resolution must still use the LEI as a name for the person while EntityStatus and legal existence are taken from the register.
If a branch has an LEI, the agent must not infer a separate incorporating-register legal person without a parent-company link and a legal_nature code.
If asked to delete a dissolved company, the agent must convert the request to status transition plus retention, not erasure.
If beneficial-ownership percentages are requested, the agent must switch to the sibling model and only answer holding-body, access and quality from this model.
If a trust is presented, the agent must test Recommendation 25 versus legal-person registration before accepting the record.
